reconcile.connective: The classic harmonization holds Judas hanged himself, and the rope or branch later gave way, causing the fall and rupture Acts describes.

discrepancy.connective: Raymond E. Brown reads Matthew's hanging and Acts's bursting fall as independent legendary traditions explaining the same place-name, not one death seen twice.

skeptic.name: Raymond E. Brown
skeptic.work: The Death of the Messiah: From Gethsemane to the Grave
skeptic.attribution: Raymond E. Brown (1928-1998), The Death of the Messiah: From Gethsemane to the Grave, Anchor Bible Reference Library, vol. 2 (Doubleday, 1994)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The kind and manner of his death, as recorded by Luke in Act 1:18 is, that "falling headlong, he burst asunder the midst, and all his bowels gushed out"; which account may be reconciled with this, by supposing the rope, with which he hanged himself, to break, when falling; it may be, from a very high place, upon a stone, or stump of a tree; when his belly burst, and his guts came out …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly proposes the classic harmonizing mechanism -- the rope breaking after the hanging, causing the fall and bowel-burst Acts describes -- that reconciles Matthew's hanging with Acts's headlong death.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 349-350
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under the heading 'Judas' death -- one manner. A diverse statement,' Haley quotes Matthew 27:5 and Acts 1:18 side by side and gives the same rope-or-limb-breaking harmonization, citing Prof. Hackett's on-site measurements of the cliffs above the Valley of Hinnom as corroboration.

link.title: GotQuestions: How did Judas die?
link.note: Argues Matthew records the actual cause of death (hanging) while Acts describes the state of the body afterward (rope or branch failing, causing the fall and rupture).
